title: General-Purpose Pseudorandom Generators — Definition 2.1

reading.text: Self-contained lesson. Optional background: Goldreich's Primer, Ch. 2 (PRG definition)

body:
## Definition 2.1: the basic definition

Chapter 2 formalizes **general-purpose pseudorandom generators**.
Loosely speaking, they are efficient deterministic programs that expand short randomly selected seeds into longer pseudorandom bit sequences, where "pseudorandom" means computationally indistinguishable from truly random by any efficient algorithm.
Identifying efficiency with polynomial time, the generator is a fixed algorithm working within some fixed polynomial time, whereas the distinguisher may be *any* polynomial-time algorithm — potentially more complex than the generator.

@def:prg
## Reading the quantifiers (slowly)

The order matters, and each piece earns its place:

- **$\forall D$ (probabilistic polynomial-time):** every efficient distinguisher is covered; none may succeed.
- **$\forall p$ (positive polynomial):** the gap must be smaller than the reciprocal of *every* positive polynomial — a gap of 1/10 is not enough, since $p(k) = 10$ is a positive polynomial.
- **$\exists \ell$ with $\ell(k) > k$:** the generator stretches strictly; larger $\ell$ is more useful, but the definition only requires the strict inequality.
- **$\forall$ sufficiently large $k$:** finitely many small cases may misbehave; only the tail matters.

The function $d(k) = |\Pr[D(G(U_k)){=}1] - \Pr[D(U_{\ell(k)}){=}1]|$ is the **distinguishing gap** of $D$.
Definition 2.1 requires this gap to be a **negligible** function: smaller than the reciprocal of any positive polynomial, for all but finitely many $k$ (see @def:negligible).

## The archetypical application: Construction 2.2 & Proposition 2.3

Why this exact definition?shows the pay-off: a PRG is a *universal randomness compressor* — one generator reduces the randomness complexity of every efficient randomized algorithm, and Proposition 2.3 proves the substitution is undetectable.

**Construction 2.2 (typical application of pseudorandom generators).**
An algorithm $A$ uses $\rho(n)$ truly random bits on inputs of length $n$ — write $A(x; r)$ for the run on input $x$ with coin tosses $r \in \{0,1\}^{\rho(n)}$. We replace those random bits by pseudorandom ones.

The idea, in one sentence: **run $A$ on the first $\rho(n)$ bits of $G(s)$ instead of on truly random $r$.** The only requirement is that the seed is long enough — the stretch function must satisfy $\ell(k) \ge \rho(n)$, so that $G(s)$ has at least $\rho(n)$ bits to hand out.

> On input $x$: pick the smallest $k$ with $\ell(k) \ge \rho(n)$, sample $s \leftarrow \{0,1\}^k$, and output $A(x; r)$ where $r$ is the $\rho(n)$-bit prefix of $G(s)$. Call this algorithm $A_G$.

Since $G$ runs in polynomial time and $k = \ell^{-1}(\rho(n))$ is polynomial, $A_G$ is still efficient — but its **randomness complexity drops from $\rho$ to $\ell^{-1} \circ \rho$**: with $\ell(k) = k^2$, from $\rho(n)$ to $\sqrt{\rho(n)}$.

Why is this legitimate? If some input made $A_G$'s output distribution differ noticeably from $A$'s, that difference would distinguish $G(U_k)$ from $U_{\ell(k)}$ — exactly what pseudorandomness forbids. So one generator $G$ safely substitutes for the random coins of *every* efficient randomized algorithm.

@thm:prop23

**What this says in words.** $F$ represents a potential attempt to *find* an input $x$ on which the output of $A_G$ is distinguishable from the output of $A$ (the attempt may be benign — a user feeding $A_G$ inputs from some application — or adversarial — inputs supplied by a malicious party). $T$ represents the potential *use* of the output: given $x$ and a sample of either $A_G(x) = A(x, U_{k(|x|)})$ or $A(x) = A(x, U_{\rho(|x|)})$, $T$ tries to tell which one it saw. The proposition says the expected absolute difference, over inputs $F$ finds, is negligible. If $A$ is a decision procedure, it is infeasible to find an $x$ on which $A_G$ decides differently from $A$; if $A$ is a search procedure for an NP-relation, it is infeasible to find an $x$ on which $A_G$ outputs a wrong solution.
## A warning: ad-hoc tests are not enough

"Pseudo-random number generators" appeared with the first computers, but typical implementations only pass some **ad-hoc statistical test**.
The Primer warns that passing some statistical tests does not mean the generator will pass a new test or be good for a future, untested application.
Definition 2.1 is designed for the general result: *for all practical purposes, using the output of the generator is as good as using truly unbiased coin tosses*, because computational indistinguishability covers all possible efficient applications (see @def:prg).

defs.name: General-purpose pseudorandom generator (Definition 2.1)
defs.statement:
**Definition 2.1 (general-purpose pseudorandom generator).** A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm $G$ is called a pseudorandom generator if there exists a stretch function `ℓ: ℕ → ℕ` (satisfying `ℓ(k) > k` for all $k$) such that for any probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm $D$, any positive polynomial $p$, and all sufficiently large $k$:

$$|\Pr[D(G(U_k)){=}1] - \Pr[D(U_{\ell(k)}){=}1]| < 1/p(k)$$

where $U_n$ denotes the uniform distribution over $\{0,1\}^n$, and the probability is taken over $U_k$ (resp. $U_{\ell(k)}$) as well as over the internal coin tosses of $D$.
defs.intuition: One fixed polynomial-time generator whose output no efficient algorithm can tell apart from truly random bits.

defs.name: Negligible function
defs.statement: A function $\mu: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ is negligible if it vanishes faster than the reciprocal of any positive polynomial: for every positive polynomial $p$ and all sufficiently large $k$, $\mu(k) < 1/p(k)$.
defs.intuition: An event with negligible probability stays negligible even after a feasible (polynomial) number of repetitions.

theorems.name: Proposition 2.3: the substitution is undetectable
theorems.statement:
**Proposition 2.3.** Let $A$, $\rho$ and $G$ be as in Construction 2.2, and suppose that $\rho: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is 1-1. Then, for every pair of probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms — a **finder** $F$ and a **tester** $T$ — every positive polynomial $p$, and all sufficiently long $n$:

$$\sum_{x \in \{0,1\}^n} \Pr[F(1^n){=}x] \cdot \left|\Delta_{A,T}(x)\right| < \frac{1}{p(n)}$$

where

$$\Delta_{A,T}(x) \;=\; \Pr[T(x,\, A(x,\, U_{\rho(|x|)})){=}1] - \Pr[T(x,\, A_G(x,\, U_{k(|x|)})){=}1]$$

and the probabilities are taken over the $U_m$'s as well as over the internal coin tosses of $F$ and $T$.
theorems.intuition: No efficient method can locate an input where the pseudorandom substitution is noticeable, so one universal generator safely replaces the coin tosses of every efficient randomized application.
theorems.proof:
Any triple $(A, F, T)$ violating the claim can be converted into an algorithm $D$ that distinguishes $G(U_k)$ from $U_{\ell(k)}$, contradicting pseudorandomness. The key observation: for every $x \in \{0,1\}^n$,

$$\Delta_{A,T}(x) = \Pr[T(x,\, A(x,\, U_{\rho(n)})){=}1] - \Pr[T(x,\, A(x,\, G'(U_{k(n)}))){=}1]$$

where $G'(s)$ is the $\rho(n)$-bit prefix of $G(s)$. So a method for finding $x$ with large $|\Delta_{A,T}(x)|$ yields a distinguisher: given a sample $r \in \{0,1\}^{\ell(k(n))}$, output $T(x, A(x, r'))$, where $r'$ is the $\rho(n)$-bit prefix of $r$.

*Warm-up version:* $D$ on input $r$ obtains $x \leftarrow F(1^n)$, computes $y = A(x, r')$, and outputs $T(x, y)$. Then $D(U_{\ell(k(n))}) \equiv T(X_n, A(X_n, U_{\rho(n)}))$ and $D(G(U_{k(n)})) \equiv T(X_n, A(X_n, G'(U_{k(n)})))$ with $X_n = F(1^n)$, so

$$\Pr[D(U_{\ell(k(n))}){=}1] - \Pr[D(G(U_{k(n)})){=}1] = \mathbb{E}[\Delta_{A,T}(F(1^n))]$$

which must be negligible — giving the weaker claim with $\mathbb{E}[\Delta]$ instead of $\mathbb{E}[|\Delta|]$.

*Handling the absolute value:* the trouble is that $\Delta_{A,T}(x)$ may be positive on some $x$'s and negative on others, so $\mathbb{E}[\Delta]$ can be small by cancellation even when $\mathbb{E}[|\Delta|]$ is large. Fix: determine the sign of $\Delta_{A,T}(x)$ at $x = F(1^n)$ and flip $D$'s output accordingly — output $T(x, A(x, r'))$ if $\Delta_{A,T}(x) > 0$ and $1 - T(x, A(x, r'))$ otherwise. Then every $x$ contributes $|\Delta_{A,T}(x)|$ to $D$'s distinguishing gap. Determining the sign is only needed when $|\Delta_{A,T}(x)|$ is large, which is a feasible (approximation) task; details in [19, Sec. 8.2.2]. ∎

checkpoints.question: Which statement is NOT part of Definition 2.1?

options.text: G is deterministic and runs in polynomial time.
There is a stretch function ℓ with ℓ(k) > k for all k.
The stretch satisfies ℓ(k) ≥ 2^k for all k.
G(U_k) and U_{ℓ(k)} are computationally indistinguishable.

checkpoints.explanation: Definition 2.1 only requires ℓ(k) > k; larger stretch is more useful, but the definition makes no requirement beyond strict stretching. In fact ℓ is upper-bounded by the generator's running time (hence by a polynomial), so ℓ(k) ≥ 2^k is impossible for a polynomial-time generator. Determinism, polynomial time, and computational indistinguishability from uniform are exactly the three ingredients of the definition.

checkpoints.question: Which reading of Definition 2.1 is correct?

options.text: For every PPT distinguisher D and every positive polynomial p, for all sufficiently large k: |Pr[D(G(U_k))=1] − Pr[D(U_{ℓ(k)})=1]| < 1/p(k).
There exists a PPT distinguisher D and a polynomial p such that the gap is < 1/p(k) for all k.
For every PPT distinguisher D, there is a polynomial p (depending on D) with gap < 1/p(k) for all k.
For all k and all p: |Pr[D(G(U_k))=1] − Pr[D(U_{ℓ(k)})=1]| < 1/p(k) for every distinguisher D.

checkpoints.explanation: The quantifier order is ∀D ∀p ∀ sufficiently large k: the gap must be smaller than the reciprocal of every positive polynomial, for every PPT distinguisher, on all but finitely many k. A single p (option B), or a p chosen after D (option C), weakens the requirement by allowing a fixed non-negligible gap. Option D demands the inequality even for tiny k, which the definition explicitly does not require: only the tail matters.

exercises.prompt: Restate Definition 2.1 from memory with the full quantifier structure. Then explain why the distinguisher may be more complex (run longer) than the generator.
exercises.hint: The generator is one fixed polynomial-time algorithm; the distinguisher is any polynomial-time algorithm. Reread the paragraphs right after Definition 2.1.

exercises.prompt: Describe Construction 2.2: given a PRG G with stretch ℓ and a PPT algorithm A with randomness complexity ρ(n), how does the derived algorithm A_G work, and what does Proposition 2.3 guarantee?
exercises.hint: A_G picks a seed of length k where ℓ(k) ≥ ρ(|x|) and feeds A the ρ(|x|)-bit prefix of G(s). The guarantee is about the infeasibility of finding an input where A_G's behavior differs from A's.

before.question: The range of G has only 2^k outputs inside a space of 2^{ℓ(k)} strings — how could such a sparse set look uniform?

options.text: Because "uniform-looking" is defined computationally: an ensemble is pseudorandom when it is indistinguishable from the uniform ensemble by every efficient algorithm (§2.3.1), and sparsity alone gives no efficient test an edge.
It cannot — any sparse set can be told apart from uniform by a simple counting test that runs in polynomial time.
Because 2^k / 2^{ℓ(k)} is close to 1 whenever the stretch ℓ(k) − k is small.
Because G outputs every string in its range with the same probability, which makes its output distribution exactly uniform.

before.explanation: Definition 2.1 requires only that no probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm can tell G(U_k) apart from U_{ℓ(k)}: the distinguishing gap must be negligible for every PPT distinguisher (§2.1). The range's density 2^k / 2^{ℓ(k)} is exponentially small, but detecting the sparsity would require an efficient procedure that exploits the tiny range — which the definition rules out. As §2.3.1 remarks, an ensemble that is indistinguishable from the uniform ensemble is exactly what is called pseudorandom.

after.question: What is the density of the range, 2^k / 2^{ℓ(k)}, and why does that sparsity not contradict pseudorandomness?

options.text: The density is 2^k / 2^{ℓ(k)} = 2^{-(ℓ(k)−k)}; it does not contradict pseudorandomness because pseudorandomness is defined by indistinguishability from the uniform ensemble under all efficient algorithms, not by the density of the range (§2.1, §2.3.1).
The density is 2^{ℓ(k)} / 2^k = 2^{ℓ(k)−k}, which is large enough to make the output distribution look uniform.
The density is 1, because G maps each seed to a distinct output and every output is equally likely.
The density is 2^{-k}, so the range is dense inside {0,1}^{ℓ(k)}.

after.explanation: The range of G contains 2^k strings inside the ambient space {0,1}^{ℓ(k)} of size 2^{ℓ(k)}, so the density is 2^k / 2^{ℓ(k)} = 2^{-(ℓ(k)−k)} — astronomically small when the stretch is large. Pseudorandomness never requires the range to be dense: §2.3.1 defines an ensemble as pseudorandom exactly when it is computationally indistinguishable from the uniform ensemble. Sparsity only matters if an efficient algorithm can exploit it, and Definition 2.1 guarantees that none can.
